If $F$ is a vector field and $C$ is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of $F$ across $C$ is given by

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s,
$$

where $n$ denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to $C.$ In this case, we have

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s+{\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s,
$$

where the sides ${C}_{i}$ and unit vectors ${n}_{i}$ are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14234550/assets/00a9df76d0be8ffd33b2ee968b57a21eb1e6947af6e94505313f163b584f5769.png)

We compute this integral in two stages. 

- First, consider the side ${C}_{1}.$ We have that ${n}_{1}=i,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{1}}(-3x\,i-2y\,j)\cdot i\,\text{d}s \\  & =-3{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{1},$ we have

$$
r(t)=2i+t\,j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=j,\,t\in [-1,1].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-3{\int }_{{C}_{1}}x\,\text{d}s & =-3{\int }_{-1}^{1}2\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-6{\int }_{-1}^{1}\text{d}t \\  & =(-6)\cdot 2 \\  & =-12.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{3}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{1}}F\cdot {n}_{1}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{3}}F\cdot {n}_{3}\,\text{d}s=-12.
$$

- Next, we consider the side ${C}_{2}.$ We have that ${n}_{2}=j,$ and therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{C}_{2}}(-3x\,i-2y\,j)\cdot j\,\text{d}s \\  & =-2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s.\end{aligned}
$$

This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side ${C}_{2},$ we have

$$
r(t)=t\,i+j,\,⇒\,{r}^{′}(t)=i,\,t\in [-2,2].
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}-2{\int }_{{C}_{2}}y\,\text{d}s & =-2{\int }_{-2}^{2}1\cdot ||{r}^{′}(t)||\,\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{-2}^{2}\text{d}t \\  & =(-2)\cdot 4 \\  & =-8.\end{aligned}
$$

By symmetry, the flux integral across the side ${C}_{4}$ must be the same. Therefore,

$$
{\int }_{{C}_{2}}F\cdot {n}_{2}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{C}_{4}}F\cdot {n}_{4}\,\text{d}s=-8.
$$

Finally, then

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot n\,\text{d}s=2\cdot (-12)+2\cdot (-8)=-40.
$$
html:
If F is a vector field and C is a piecewise-smooth, simple, closed curve, then the flux of F across C is given by ∮CF⋅nds, where n denotes the outward-pointing unit normal vector to C. In this case, we have

∮CF⋅nds=∫C1F⋅n1ds+∫C2F⋅n2ds+∫C3F⋅n3ds+∫C4F⋅n4ds,

where the sides Ci and unit vectors ni are shown below.

We compute this integral in two stages.

  • First, consider the side C1. We have that n1=i, and therefore, ∫C1F⋅n1ds=∫C1(−3xi−2yj)⋅ids=−3∫C1xds. This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side C1, we have r(t)=2i+tj,⇒r′(t)=j,t∈[−1,1]. Therefore, −3∫C1xds=−3∫−112⋅||r′(t)||dt=−6∫−11dt=(−6)⋅2=−12. By symmetry, the flux integral across the side C3 must be the same. Therefore, ∫C1F⋅n1ds=∫C3F⋅n3ds=−12.
  • Next, we consider the side C2. We have that n2=j, and therefore, ∫C2F⋅n2ds=∫C2(−3xi−2yj)⋅jds=−2∫C2yds. This is a line integral with respect to arc length, which we can evaluate in the usual way. Parameterizing the side C2, we have r(t)=ti+j,⇒r′(t)=i,t∈[−2,2]. Therefore, −2∫C2yds=−2∫−221⋅||r′(t)||dt=−2∫−22dt=(−2)⋅4=−8. By symmetry, the flux integral across the side C4 must be the same. Therefore, ∫C2F⋅n2ds=∫C4F⋅n4ds=−8.

Finally, then

∮CF⋅nds=2⋅(−12)+2⋅(−8)=−40.
